doc.title: Lonnie Liston Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 9, 2021

title: Learning tunes on the bandstand in Baltimore jam sessions
summary: Jam sessions at the North End Lounge were a second school; older players and bass players called out changes.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: So it’s just basic standards. I wasn’t writing back then. So but the North End Lounge, all the jazz groups when they came in town they would come by and do jam sessions. So like you know, so I was really in school in another way, both schools at the same time.
Yes. This time was formative for you as a bunch of years before the real books came on the scene.
So if you had to learn a tune, how did you go about doing that?

Well we used to listen to the records or some of the older guys would know the changes, the chord changes. Because it was funny, you know we used to go sit in with the older guys and sometimes you know the bass player would have to be telling you the chord changes while you’re playing. That was interesting, because I remember when you’re in school they would say okay C minor with a diminished fifth. Or C minor with a augmented fifth. But see when you’re on the bandstand you have a tempo. So they say C minor flat five. Or F7 plus — so it was good. And like I say it was two different schools at the same time.
